first_impression.reaction: Our daughter sent this because Costa Rica has come up. Geoff's first question will be whether it's legal, and the first lines answer it: 'It will.' I read it all on the iPad. It's careful and it doesn't hide anything, but some of what it says frightened me: kidnappings, crocodiles, malaria and Zika, all in one page. The questions to ask the resort are the best part, with contracts, currency, deposits and step-free access all in there. What I still don't know is who looks after us over there, because the nearest proper Australian embassy is in Mexico City. I also can't tell whether the children would need to fly over twice just to sign a form.

journey.quote: Costa Rica is on your shortlist, and before you choose a coast or a resort you want to know one thing: will the marriage stand? It will.
journey.reaction: Good. That's Geoff's first question, and it's answered in the first two lines. I can send him this paragraph as it is.

journey.section: Can Australians marry legally in Costa Rica?
journey.quote: It does not recognise an overseas marriage where either person is already married to someone else, is not old enough to marry, is too closely related to the other, or is forced to marry.
journey.reaction: Plain and clear. None of those apply to us, so I can stop worrying about whether it counts at home.

journey.section: Before you go: entry and documents
journey.quote: Smartraveller rates Costa Rica at level 2, "Exercise a high degree of caution", due to the threat of violent crime, and notes that carjackings and "express kidnappings" are increasingly common.
journey.reaction: Well, that stopped me. I'm glad it's honest and it's quoting the government, not making it up. But I'm now picturing my mother in an airport car at night. I'd want to know who is meeting the family off the plane.

journey.section: Before you go: entry and documents
journey.quote: Read the full [Smartraveller advice for Costa Rica](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/americas/costa-rica) before you book,.
journey.reaction: There's a stray comma before the full stop. A small thing, but I notice these, and on a serious page about legal papers it makes me wonder who checked it.

journey.section: Before you go: entry and documents
journey.quote: Australia has a consulate in San José headed by an Honorary Consul, which provides limited consular assistance; full consular assistance comes from the Australian Embassy in Mexico City.
journey.reaction: Mexico City. So if someone is in hospital or a passport goes missing at 2am, who do I ring? This is the question I keep asking, and the page makes it more pressing.

journey.section: Before you go: entry and documents
journey.quote: Seriously ill or injured travellers may need medical evacuation, so your travel insurance must cover it.
journey.reaction: Sensible, and I'll make sure Mum's policy covers it. It speaks to the couple, though. I'd have liked it to mention parents and older guests as well.

journey.section: The documents you gather at home
journey.quote: That one-month window shapes your timeline more than anything else on the list, so order this certificate last.
journey.reaction: Practical. That's the kind of mistake that costs money and a second trip to the post office. I'll tell her.

journey.quote: You then present yourselves together and both sign the request.
journey.reaction: In person? Then four to six months later they come back to marry? I read it twice. Does that mean two trips to Costa Rica? The page says to ask, which is fair, but it's a big cost if it's true.

journey.quote: There is no charge for the registry service of celebrating the marriage.
journey.reaction: Nice to see something free. But the notice, the translations, the apostilles and the notary all cost something, and none of it has a figure.

journey.quote: Are you in good standing with the Dirección Nacional de Notariado, with an enabled user in the TSE's system?
journey.reaction: I like this. It's what I'd want to ask anyone taking our money overseas: are you properly registered? Though I'd rather someone on our side checked it than the children doing it in Spanish.

journey.section: Ceremonies on the beach, in the rainforest or at your resort
journey.quote: If you picture vows on a headland lawn or under a rainforest canopy, the setting rests on your notary, or on a symbolic ceremony after the legal signing.
journey.reaction: Clearer than some of these guides. Office for the government route, the notary if they want the legal part at the resort. I understood it on the first read.

journey.section: Ceremonies on the beach, in the rainforest or at your resort
journey.quote: Strong currents and rip tides occur on the Caribbean and Pacific coasts, lifeguards and warning signs may be absent on public beaches, and crocodile attacks have been reported on the Pacific coast.
journey.reaction: Crocodiles. Honest again, and I'd rather know. But by now the list of dangers is long, and Geoff will read this line out loud at dinner.

journey.section: When to marry in Costa Rica
journey.quote: The paperwork sets its own calendar. Count back from your date: the Registro Civil's average of 4 to 6 months, a civil status certificate no more than a month old, and 25 working days of registration afterwards.
journey.reaction: Useful. One sentence I can hold on to. I'd have liked the dry months spelled out just as plainly, rather than me working it out from what the wet season is.

journey.quote: Public medical facilities are limited in smaller towns and rural areas.
journey.reaction: That decides it for our family: somewhere near a proper hospital and not a long drive on unsealed roads. Thank you for saying it.

journey.quote: **Security:** how does your security team work with our private security?
journey.reaction: Private security? We're a family from Glen Waverley, not celebrities. This list feels written for someone else. Drones and outside photographers too. I skipped past it.

journey.quote: **Deposits and contracts:** whose name is on the contract, in which language is it written, in which currency are payments made, and when do deposits become non-refundable?
journey.reaction: There it is. Name, language, currency, deposits. This is exactly what I'd ask, and it's in writing. My favourite line on the page.

journey.quote: **Access:** which ceremony, dining and guest spaces are step-free?
journey.reaction: Yes. Mum and her walking frame. Someone thought about us.

journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor, start to finish, holds the whole plan together, from venue and travel to vendors and payments.
journey.reaction: One person who handles the payments. That's what I want when it's our money. I'd like a name and a phone number, though.

journey.section: Plan your Costa Rica wedding with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor works in your time zone, quotes in AUD, and agrees the fee in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: AUD and the fee in writing, good. But Melbourne time isn't Costa Rica time. Who is looking after things over there on the day, given the embassy is in another country?

unanswered_questions: With only an Honorary Consul in San José and the embassy in Mexico City, who do the couple (or I) ring if something goes wrong outside Melbourne business hours? Is anyone from Wedded Wonderland on the ground on the day? (deferred business detail)
Who meets the family at the airport and drives them to the resort in daylight, including a guest with a walking frame? Do you arrange transfers? (deferred business detail)
Do the couple have to fly to Costa Rica twice, once to sign the Registro Civil request and again to marry, or does a notary avoid that? The page leaves it as 'ask'.
Are our deposits protected if a Costa Rican resort or supplier, or Wedded Wonderland itself, fails?
Will Wedded Wonderland handle the Spanish paperwork, translations, notary checks and apostilles, or is that all on the couple? (deferred business detail)
Roughly what do the La Gaceta notice, the notary, the translations and the apostilles cost, and in what currency? (fee amounts deferred)
How is your fee charged, roughly what range, and do you receive commissions from Costa Rican resorts? (deferred business detail)
Have you planned real weddings in Costa Rica I could look at, and how many? (deferred business detail)
Is the first conversation a phone call with a real person, and can I join it as a parent paying part?
Are there extras or Wedded Privileges for couples who book with you? (deferred business detail)
Which months are the dry season, in plain words?

turn_offs_found.quote: Criminals often target tourist areas, resorts, transport hubs and public transport, and Smartraveller advises planning to arrive at or leave the airport during daylight hours.
turn_offs_found.why: Not a turn-off in tone. It's honest and calm, but together with kidnappings, crocodiles, malaria and Zika it leaves me frightened, and nothing straight after says who will look after the family. My fear about elderly guests abroad is raised and not answered.

turn_offs_found.quote: For a wedding of this scale, the questions to put to a resort are less about the view and more about control.
turn_offs_found.why: 'This scale' and private security made me feel I'd wandered into a page for someone much richer. It isn't slang, but it doesn't sound like it's talking to a family like ours. The deposits and access questions underneath are spot on, though.

would_share_with: My husband, the intro and 'Recognition and registering at home', to settle whether the marriage counts in Australia, plus the Mexico City embassy line with 'who do we ring?' written next to it

My daughter, the resort questions on deposits, contracts and step-free access, the 'order this certificate last' line, and the line about limited medical facilities in rural areas, so she picks somewhere with Nana in mind

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, [start a conversation with Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=getting-married-in-costa-rica&utm_content=closing).
cta_reaction.why: It's careful, and 'quotes in AUD' and 'fee in writing' are what I want. But this page has made me more nervous about Costa Rica, not less. I'd talk to Geoff first, and I'd only go ahead if it's a phone call with a real person who can tell me who is there on the day, who meets us at the airport, and how deposits are protected.

top_3_changes: After the safety and consular lines, add one calm sentence that points to the help (for example, Wedded Concierge can plan airport transfers in daylight and support on the day), but only if the business confirms it. Otherwise flag it. The run of risks currently ends with no reassurance.

Settle the 'sign the request together in person' point: say plainly whether the Registro Civil route means an earlier trip and whether the notary route avoids it, if the source pack supports it. If not, keep the 'ask' and say why it matters (a second trip).

Fix the stray comma in 'before you book,.' and soften 'For a wedding of this scale' and the private security item, or move them later, so the resort list opens with deposits, contracts and step-free access.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Journey types limited to gained_trust, lost_trust, confused, bored, excited, objection
Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent): read top to bottom on iPad, focused on deposits, who is responsible, elderly guests, insurance and a phone call
No invented brand facts; on-the-ground support, deposit protection, transfers, paperwork help, fees, commissions, real weddings and Privileges placed in unanswered_questions
VERIFY markers and HTML comments (fact tags, image slots) ignored
Deferred business details and fee amounts listed as unanswered questions, not penalised or made must-fix

open_questions.question: Does fact_02 (signing the request together in person) combined with fact_11 (4 to 6 months) mean two trips for overseas couples, and does fact_200 show the notary route avoids it? If the source doesn't settle it, flag rather than fill. Also, can the dry season months be stated plainly from fact_115 and fact_116?

assumptions: Margaret arrived via a link from her daughter, reading on an iPad, as a parent contributing about half. Relevance is 3 because the page is a legal how-to written to the couple, though it covers insurance, rural medical care and step-free access.

Likelihood to enquire is 3: the deposits, contracts and access questions earn trust, but the long list of safety risks with no named help on the ground holds her back. That help is a deferred business detail, so it is not penalised as must-fix.
Her mother's walking frame comes from the persona card's voice samples; her suburb (Glen Waverley) and husband's name (Geoff) are character colour consistent with earlier panels, not page facts.
The 3-minute budget covered the full article top to bottom, with the FAQ skimmed as it repeats the body.
